A black stone like a bean is found in the Nile, and upon seeing it, dogs do not bark. You may also carry a dog's tongue placed under your big toe in your shoe; or if you carry a dried dog's heart with you, according to Sextus <note>likely Sextus Placitus, a 4th-century medical writer</note>; or a hare's fur or dung, according to Pliny. Or you may carry the severed tail of a young weasel on your foot, or give the dog a frog in a morsel of food; all these things serve to avoid the barking of dogs. Nigidius <note>Publius Nigidius Figulus, a Roman scholar and occultist</note> says that dogs will flee the sight of a man for an entire day if he removes a tick from a pig and carries it for a little while. Oppian <note>A Greco-Roman poet known for his works on hunting and fishing</note> writes:

> But if you carry a small piece cut from the skin of a hyena,
> Immediately the puppies and fierce dogs will be
> Struck with bitter terror, and thereafter they will not
> Bark at you as you walk, even if they barked before.

### How to make it so a dog cannot run.

If you smear its paws with oil, it will be hindered in its running; it happens in this way.

### To make a hawk courageous.

You shall encourage the bird against its prey so that it attacks large birds. Moisten the meat which it uses during the time of hunting with wine; or if it is a goshawk, give it a little vinegar. When you wish it to fly, give it three morsels of meat moistened with wine, or pour wine from your own mouth into the beak of a young pigeon <note>then feed the pigeon to the hawk</note>, and then let it fly. In this way:

### You will make partridges more combative,

If you give them branches of <term>adiantum</term> <gloss>maidenhair fern</gloss> in their food, according to Pliny. And:

### Roosters are made more combative,

By giving them garlic in their food just before they are to fight; from which comes the very witty term in the Old Comedy <term>eskorodismenoi</term> <gloss>garlic-fed</gloss>, which means one who is vehement and too inclined toward a fight.

### Lest a bird fly into the heights,

Pluck out the tail feathers which direct the course upward; thus it will fly in a circle below. If you wish:

### That a bird cannot fly at all,

Cut the upper and lower nerves of the wing, and it remains without further harm; the bird will not fly, and in this way they do not escape from aviaries.

<summary>This page provides folklore and practical methods for hunters to silence dogs using charms or biological materials, and techniques to alter the temperament or physical ability of birds like hawks, partridges, and roosters.</summary>
<keywords>dog barking, animal behavior, falconry, cockfighting, Oppian, Pliny, garlic, veterinary magic, hunting charms</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>shines with piety, religion, prudence, and the worship and veneration of God, as if he had perceived the truth with his own eyes through true reason. By the confidence of his belief, he stands out among men as much as the sun surpasses the other stars by its light. For the sun itself illuminates the other stars not so much by the magnitude of its power as by its divinity and holiness. Believe this sun to be the second god, O Asclepius, governing all other things and illuminating all worldly creatures, whether they possess a soul or are inanimate.

For if the world is a living being <note>original: "animal mundus"</note> that is always alive, and was, and is, and shall be, then nothing in the world is mortal. Since every single part of a living being is in the world itself, as if in one and the same animal that is always living, there is no place for mortality. Therefore, God himself must be most full of life and eternity, if it is necessary for him to live forever. Thus the sun, just like the world, is sempiternal; so too is he always the governor of living things, or the one who attends to and dispenses their entire vitality. God, therefore, is the sempiternal governor of the living beings, or the vital things, which are in the world, and he is the eternal dispenser of life itself. He dispensed this once by an eternal law, providing life to all vital things in the manner which I shall describe.

<summary>Hermes explains that the pious man excels others like the sun among stars and describes the sun as a second god that governs all life. He argues that because the world is a living, eternal being, nothing within it is truly mortal under the eternal law of God.</summary>
<keywords>piety, sun, second god, living world, immortality, eternal law, Asclepius, vitality, divine governance</keywords>

Marcus Varro <note>Marcus Terentius Varro, a prolific Roman scholar.</note> testifies that he saw these things. And there are things even more wonderful than these: for on the Attic shore, the sea sounds like a lyre. At Megara, a certain rock makes the sound of a stringed instrument when struck by pebbles, so great is the power of Music. It also soothes the soul, lifts the mind, incites warriors to war, and eases the labor and fatigue of individual tasks. It recalls those who have fallen or are in despair and comforts travelers. And the Arabs say that camels carrying burdens are comforted by their singing drivers. In a similar way, those carrying heavy loads sing, and are made more capable and relieved by it: for song produces delight and capability. It mitigates the angry, gladdens the sad and anxious, pacifies the discordant, tempers the madness of the frantic, and dissipates vain thoughts. Hence it is that Democritus and Theophrastus affirm that some diseases of the body and mind can be either cured or induced in this way. Thus we read that Terpander and Arion of Methymna <note>Arion was a legendary Greek kitharode; Methymna was a city on Lesbos.</note>...

<summary>Agrippa describes the miraculous physical effects of music on nature and its psychological power to heal, motivate, and soothe both humans and animals.</summary>
<keywords>music, harmony, Marcus Varro, Arabs, Democritus, Theophrastus, Terpander, Arion, psychology, healing</keywords>

for the good is innate to truth, along with life and light, and no further avenger has approached. Indeed, all the avengers have been cast out by a sudden impulse. You have understood, my son, the manner of this **rebirth** <note>original: "regenerationis"</note>. When the **number ten** <note>original: "denario numero"; the Decad, representing perfection and the divine powers</note> is present, the intellectual generation is complete, which rejects the **number twelve** <note>original: "duodenarium numerum"; the Duodecad, representing the twelve zodiacal vices</note>. We have observed this from the generation itself. Therefore, whoever loses their bodily senses because of the kindness of this generation, which is according to God, knows themselves to be composed of divine things. Having become steadfast, they rejoice in divine power with their whole mind.

**TATIUS.** O father, I conceive this not by the sight of my eyes, but by the action of the mind, which is exercised through inner powers. I am in heaven, in the earth, in the water, in the air. I am in animals, in trees, in the body, before the body, and after the body. But I wish you would tell me this further: how are the avenging darknesses, twelve in number, repelled by the ten powers? By what means, Trismegistus?

**HERMES.** This tabernacle, O son, is constituted from the **zodiac circle** <note>original: "ex zodiaco circulo"</note>, which consists of that number twelve. The numbers are eleven, but one is all-formed according to the ideas of nature, for the wandering and circuit of man. Thus, those avengers are in a certain way separated from one another, yet in acting they are in a certain way joined together; for example, recklessness is inseparable from wrath. Rightly, therefore, according to correct reason, they are separated by an interval as far as they are repelled by the ten powers, that is, by the number ten. The number ten, O son, is the progenitor of the soul. Indeed, Life

<summary>Hermes explains how the ten divine powers displace the twelve zodiacal vices during spiritual rebirth, leading Tatius to a state of cosmic consciousness. The passage describes the transition from a material existence governed by the stars to a divine existence governed by the Decad.</summary>
<keywords>rebirth, Decad, Duodecad, Zodiac, Tatius, Hermes Trismegistus, cosmic consciousness, spiritual generation</keywords>

and it will mix itself with the waters of its own fountain. There are, therefore, gods who are the chiefs of all species. These are followed by the gods whose chief is <term>ousia</term> <gloss>essence or being</gloss>. These are the sensible gods, similar to their dual origin, who produce all things through sensible nature, each one illuminating his own work through the other. Of the heaven, or whatever is comprised by that name, the <term>ousiarches</term> <gloss>ruler of essence</gloss> is Jupiter <margin>Jupiter.</margin>. For through the heaven, Jupiter provides life to all things. Of the sun, the <term>ousiarches</term> is light <margin>Light.</margin>. For the good of light is infused into us through the orb of the sun. There are thirty-six <note>referring to the decans of the zodiac</note> whose name is <term>Horoscopij</term> <gloss>Horoscopes or markers of the hour</gloss> <margin>Horoscopes.</margin>, who are always fixed in the same place of the stars. Their <term>ousiarches</term> or prince is he whom they call <term>Pantomorphos</term> <gloss>All-formed</gloss> <margin>All-formed.</margin> or Omniform, who creates diverse forms from diverse species. The seven spheres which are called "erratic" <note>the seven wandering planets: Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Sun, and Moon</note> have their own <term>ousiarchas</term>, that is, their own princes, whom they call Fortune or <term>Heimarmene</term> <gloss>Fate</gloss>, by whom all things are changed by the law of nature with the firmest stability and varied by eternal agitation. The air, however, is the organ or the machine of all things, through which all things are made. Moreover, the <term>ousiarches</term> of this is the second <note>referring to a secondary creative power or demiurge</note>, providing mortal things to mortals and things similar to them. These things being so, moving from the lowest to the highest, all things pertaining to themselves are so naturally connected to each other that mortal things are annexed to mortals and sensible things to sensibles. Yet the sum of the governance obeys that highest Lord, so that they are not many, but rather one. For since all things hang from the one, and rather flow down from him, when they are seen at a distance, they are believed to be many and divided. But united, they are one, or rather two: that from which all things are made, and he by whom they are made. That is, from the matter of which they are made, and by the will of him by whose nod other things are effected. ASCLEPIUS: What is this reason again, O Trismegistus? TRISMEGISTUS: It is such, O Asclepius. For God, or the Father, or the Lord...

<summary>Trismegistus explains the hierarchy of divine governors, including Jupiter as the ruler of heaven and the All-formed ruler of the fixed stars, emphasizing that all diverse forces are ultimately connected to a single divine source.</summary>
<keywords>Ousiarches, Jupiter, Pantomorphos, Fate, Heimarmene, Seven Spheres, Unity of God, Matter, Asclepius</keywords>

brought itself forth. For indeed, arsenic can by no means be fixed unless the artist-operator has an equal knowledge of its coloring spirit <note>original: "spiritū eius tingentem"; the volatile essence responsible for the chemical change</note>, a point on which all the philosophers have slumbered, striving in vain to produce anything from it. Whoever, therefore, is ignorant of this spirit, let him have no hope of fixing the substance itself, nor of attributing to it the power by which he might acquire the perfection of transmutation. For this reason, I make it known to all that the whitening of which mention has been made was drawn from a false foundation; by it, copper is falsely whitened, not transformed. The Sophists mixed <term>Venus</term> <gloss>copper</gloss> masked and painted in this manner with twice its weight of <term>Luna</term> <gloss>silver</gloss>, and sold it to goldsmiths and coin-makers. In the end, they transformed themselves into counterfeiters—not only those who sold it, but also those who bought it. Some of the Sophists took red arsenic in place of the white, and this likewise resulted in a false art. For in whatever way it is prepared, it shows nothing but whiteness. Some proceeded further to common sulfur, which they cooked as a yellow substance with vinegar, lye, or the sharpest urines, day and night, until a white color emerged. Afterward, they raised it from common salt and lime of eggs <note>calcium oxide or powdered eggshells</note> through sublimation; they cooked and sublimated it many times. Nevertheless, it always remained combustible, even though it was white. With it, however, they attempted to fix crude mercury

<summary>Paracelsus warns that arsenic cannot be fixed without understanding its spirit and exposes how "Sophists" use it to create deceptive, surface-level whitening of copper to defraud goldsmiths. He also describes failed attempts to whiten sulfur using acidic washes and sublimation.</summary>

<keywords>arsenic, fixation, transmutation, copper, silver, counterfeiting, sulfur, sublimation, mercury</keywords>

they ought to have taken, they instead took <term>pyrite</term>, <term>sulfur</term>, <term>salt</term>, <term>metal</term>, and various other materials in which there is no operation; these are expensive things from the shops, yet in the labor they are of no value at all. Our material, however, is bought from no shop, yet it is found daily in such places, and merchants cast it out into the streets. It is sufficient, therefore, that it be found for free. But the material of our <term>stone</term> <gloss>the Philosopher's Stone</gloss> is compared to all those things with which the craftsmen labor. For our stone is <term>our salt</term>, <term>our Mercury</term>, <term>verdigris</term> <gloss>copper rust</gloss>, <term>saltpeter</term>, <term>sal ammoniac</term>, <term>Mars</term> <gloss>iron</gloss>, <term>sulfur</term>, and infinite other things of that kind, yet it is not dug out from wild and rural mountains with hammers and other instruments. Instead, our stone is extracted only from our mountains and springs. In our <term>Salt-spring</term> our <term>Salt</term> is found; from our earth our metal, <term>Mercury</term>, and <term>sulfur</term> are smelted, and not from wild, foreign, and rural mountains. The craftsmen do not understand all these things, nor can they believe or comprehend them; for the Lord has darkened and stopped up their senses. For this reason, they have used these things otherwise than they ought to have been, and have missed the mark entirely. Nevertheless, they persisted in that contrary sense and followed their own stubborn heads. For instance, while they ought to have <term>distilled</term> gently, they <term>sublimated</term> <gloss>vaporized solids</gloss> there with a strong fire, scorched <term>strong waters</term> <gloss>acids</gloss>, and immediately burned the operation of nature and its substances, reducing them to nothing. Also, when they ought to have <term>dissolved</term>, they <term>coagulated</term> <gloss>solidified</gloss> there, and again, like men unskilled in things, they handled the matter unskillfully. They fell into doubt and repeatedly claimed with lying words that the art was not true but false, in which, however, they themselves are deservedly lying. For their own ignorance has shamefully deceived them, which must be imputed to their own obscure and murky cleverness, while, according to their own dark understanding, they interpreted the words differently than they sounded. For example, when the Philosophers spoke of <term>calcining</term> <gloss>reducing to powder by heat</gloss> (which they call grinding), then those unskilled <term>Philosophasters</term> <gloss>pretenders to philosophy</gloss> understood it as burning, and reduced things entirely to ashes, so that nothing could be made from them. Also, when the Philosophers <term>dissolve</term>, or transmute into water, then those <term>know-it-alls</term> <gloss>literally: those with big noses</gloss> burned nature with <term>strong water</term> <gloss>acid</gloss>, and with that same water, which has no

<summary>The author distinguishes between the common materials of the shops and the true, free material of the Alchemical Stone. He criticizes "Philosophasters" for misinterpreting metaphorical terms like calcination and dissolution, leading to failed experiments.</summary>
<keywords>Philosopher's Stone, Salt, Mercury, Sulfur, Calcination, Distillation, Philosophasters, Strong Water, Alchemy</keywords>

# FOURTH PART OF THE FIRST BOOK

requires a moderation of the fire, and a gradual succession of its increase, with caution, until it is fixed in its lime <note>original: "calce"</note>, so that it does not easily return into a body <note>revert to a metallic state</note>, in order that a greater fire may be administered to it for the perfection of its lime. Similarly, let him not happen to err regarding Jupiter <note>Tin</note>, because of its difficult reduction <note>the process of returning a calcined metal to its metallic form</note>; so that if he should ever put its lime to reduction, it might happen that it does not reduce, but he finds it in its prior disposition or turned into glass <note>original: "in uitrum redactam"</note>, and he might judge its reduction to be impossible. For we say that if one does not apply a great fire in the reduction of Jupiter, it will not reduce. If, however, he applies a great one, it does not necessarily happen that he reduces it, but it is possible to reduce it into vitrification <note>the process of turning into glass</note>. And this is because Jupiter <margin>am ta</margin> has a fugitive substance of quicksilver <note>original: "argenti uiui"</note> enclosed in the depths of its nature. If this substance endures a long delay in the fire, it will flee, and leave the body deprived of humidity, so that it is found to be converted more readily to vitrification than to the fusion of a metallic body. For everything deprived of its own humidity gives no fusion except a vitrifying one. Therefore, it necessarily remains that he must hasten to reduce it quickly with a very swift force of fire. For otherwise it is not reduced. Let him therefore be practiced in this, and he shall know.

The second method <gloss>secundus</gloss> of calcination for these <gloss>Saturn and Jupiter</gloss> two bodies, which is perfected by the sharpness of salt, is that a quantity of salt be thrown upon their surface, quantity after quantity very often during its fusion, and they should be mixed with much stirring by an iron rod <margin>wooden. boiling. see page 57, 14.</margin> over the fire, until through the mixing of salt they are turned into ash. And afterwards, by the same method of perfection, their lime may be perfected, with its own considerations. But in this there is also a difference in the calcination of these two bodies. Because lead <note>original: "plumbum"</note> is converted to powder more easily from the first labors of calcination than Jupiter <note>Tin</note>, yet its lime is not perfected more easily than that of Jupiter. The cause of this depends on the fact that Saturn <note>Lead</note> has a more fixed humidity than Jupiter.

829. Since Religion resides in the highest parts of a man, and from those highest parts his lower parts live and shine, and because **Mohammed** <note>original: "Mahumedes"</note> is present in their minds along with their Religion, someone representing Mohammed is always placed in their sight. So that they may turn their faces toward the East, over which the Lord is, he is placed below the Christian **Center** <gloss>the middle point of the spiritual world where Christians dwell</gloss>. This is not the actual Mohammed who wrote the **Koran** <note>original: "Alcoranum"</note>, but another who performs his office; nor is it always the same person, for he is changed. Once it was a man from Saxony who, having been captured by Algerians and becoming a Mohammedan, and because he had also been a Christian, was sometimes moved to speak with them about the Lord, saying that He was not the son of Joseph but the Son of God Himself. Other men succeeded this Mohammed afterward. In the place where that representative Mohammed has his seat, a fire appears like torches so that he may be known; but that fire is not visible to any others except the Mohammedans.

830. The actual Mohammed who wrote the Koran does not come into view today. I was told that in the earliest times he presided over them, but because he wished to rule over all things of their Religion as a God, he was ejected from his seat, which he held beneath the Roman Catholics, and sent down to the right side near the south. Once, a certain society of Mohammedans was incited by malicious spirits to acknowledge Mohammed as God; to settle the sedition, Mohammed was brought up from the lower earth and shown, and then I also saw him. He appeared similar to corporeal spirits who have no interior perception, with a face verging toward black, and I heard him speaking these words: *I am your Mohammed*; and soon he seemed to sink back down.

831. The Mohammedans are hostile to Christians primarily because of the faith in three Divine Persons, and the resulting worship of three Gods and as many Creators; and toward the Roman Catholics additionally because of their kneeling before images. For this reason, they call the latter Idolaters and the former fanatics, saying that they make a three-headed God, and that they say "one" but mutter "three," and thus they split Omnipotence, making three out of the one and only. They say Christians are like **Fauns** <gloss>mythological forest spirits</gloss> with three horns, one for each God, and yet three for one; and that they thus pray, thus sing, and thus sound from their pulpits.

832. The Mohammedans, like all nations who acknowledge one God and love what is just and do good from a religious motive, have their own Heaven, but it is outside the Christian one. Yet the Mohammedan Heaven is divided into two: in the lower one they live honestly with several wives, but from there none are raised into the higher Heaven except those who give up their concubines and acknowledge the Lord our Savior, and at the same time His dominion over Heaven and Hell. I heard that it is impossible for them to think that God the Father and our Lord are one, but that it is possible for them to believe that He rules over the Heavens and Hells because He is the Son of God the Father. This is the faith among them through which an ascent into the higher Heaven is granted to them by the Lord.

833. The fact that the Mohammedan Religion has been received by more kingdoms than the Christian Religion may be a stumbling block to those who think about **Divine Providence** and at the same time believe that no one can be saved except those born Christian. But the Mohammedan Religion is not a stumbling block to those who believe that all things are of Divine Providence; these people search for the reason why it is so, and they find it. It is in this: that the Mohammedan Religion acknowledges the Lord as the Greatest Prophet, the Wisest of all, and also as the Son of God; but because they have made the Koran the only book of their religion, and thus Mohammed, who wrote it, has settled in their thoughts and they follow him with some worship, they think little about our Lord. So that it may be fully known that this Religion was raised up by the Lord's Divine Providence to destroy the idolatries of many nations, it will be described in some order; but first, concerning the origin of idolatries. Before that Religion, there was **idolatrous** worship...

<summary>Swedenborg describes the state of Muslims in the spiritual world, their representative leaders, and their criticisms of Christian Trinitarianism. He explains that Islam was permitted by Divine Providence to eliminate widespread idolatry.</summary>
<keywords>Mohammedans, Islam, Koran, Divine Providence, Trinity, Idolatry, Spiritual World, Heavens, Monotheism</keywords>

If a disease or pain is inflicted Supernaturally through incantation or a Magical Impression of the Ascendants, then the healing efforts of the first three <note>the elemental, poisonous, and natural categories of medicine</note> are useless. According to Paracelsus, one must proceed Magically and Supernaturally, and the evil must be repelled in the same manner in which it was inflicted. ### On the images of the head and tail of the dragon of the Moon. Cap. XLV.

<note>A woodcut illustration depicting a serpent or dragon coiled into a circular shape resembling the Greek letter Theta (Θ). The creature has the head of a hawk and a pointed tail. Within the circular body, there is a central vertical line crossed by a shorter horizontal line, with small astrological or symbolic marks at the terminals.</note>

They also made an image of the head and tail of the dragon of the Moon <note>the lunar nodes, where the Moon's path crosses the ecliptic</note>, namely the likeness of a serpent between the aerial and fiery circle, with the head of a hawk surrounding them, in the likeness of the Greek letter <term>theta</term> <gloss>Θ</gloss>. They made it when Jupiter with the Head <note>the North Node</note> held the midheaven. They affirm that this image contributes much to the success of petitions. By this image they wished to denote a good and happy <term>daemon</term> <gloss>spirit or guiding intelligence</gloss>, and they wished to represent him by the image of a serpent. For the Egyptians and Phoenicians celebrate this as a divine animal above all others, and celebrate its divine nature because a sharper spirit and more abundant fire exists in it than in other animals. By "atmosphere," he means the **void** <note>original: *al-khalā’*, referring to the vacuum or empty space</note>, since the world could have been in a different location within that void. From this, he concluded that the world was created through **Will** <note>original: *irāda*</note>. 

The premise stating that the Will is what specifies one of two identical possibilities is correct. However, the premise stating that the world exists in a void that surrounds it is either false or not self-evident. Furthermore, his assumption of this void leads to a conclusion they find abominable: that the void would be eternal. This is because if the void were created in time, it would itself require another void in which to exist.

As for the premise stating that only a time-bound <note>original: *muḥdath*, something that begins to exist after not existing</note> object of will can result from the Will, that is not self-evident. This is because the **Will in act** <note>original: *al-irāda bi-l-fi‘l*, the actualized exercise of will</note> exists alongside the action of the **object of will** <note>original: *al-murād*</note> itself. This is because Will belongs to the category of **relative terms** <note>original: *al-muḍāf*, things that exist only in relation to one another</note>. It has been demonstrated that when one of two relative terms exists in act, the other must also exist in act, such as father and son; and if one exists in potentiality, the other exists in potentiality. Therefore, if the Will in act is created in time, the object of will must necessarily be created in time. But if the Will in act is eternal, then the object of will in act is eternal.

As for the Will that precedes the object of will, that is the **Will in potentiality** <note>original: *al-irāda bi-l-quwwa*</note>. By this, I mean a will whose object has not yet emerged into actuality, because the action that necessitates the occurrence of the object of will has not yet been joined to that will. For this reason, it is clear that when its object does emerge, the Will enters a state of existence it was not in before the object emerged into actuality, since the Will was the cause of the object's occurrence through the mediation of the action. Thus, if the **Theologians** <note>original: *al-Mutakallimūn*, scholars of *Kalām* or speculative theology</note> were to posit that the Will is created in time, it would necessarily follow that the object of will is created in time.

The apparent meaning of the **Religious Law** <note>original: *al-Shar‘*</note> is that it did not delve into such depths with the common people. For this reason, it did not explicitly state whether the Will is eternal or created in time. Rather, it stated what is most apparent: that the Will brings created beings into existence. This is found in the words of the Almighty: "Our word to a thing, when We intend it, is only that We say to it, 'Be,' and it is" <note>Quran 16:40</note>. This was expressed in this manner because the common people do not understand how created beings can result from an eternal Will. In truth, the Law did not explicitly declare the Will to be either created or eternal because this is among the <unclear>difficult matters</unclear>.

But the unlearned and those of a [base] nature, for whom it truly did not proceed from the Lord to obtain the gifts of fate, nor to have a notion of the immortal Jove <note>Jove: Jupiter, the supreme Roman deity, here used by Porphyry to refer to the highest God.</note>, not listening to both the gods and divine men, have indeed rejected all the gods; but they have chosen not only to follow the prohibited demons with no hatred, but even to revere them. While pretending to worship God, they do not perform those things alone through which God is adored. For God indeed, as the father of all, stands in need of nothing; but it is well for us when we adore him through justice and chastity and other virtues, making our very life a prayer to him through imitation and instruction concerning him. For instruction purifies, he says, and imitation deifies the affection by working toward him. He indeed preached well concerning God the Father and said by what customs he is to be worshipped. The prophetic books of the Hebrews are full of these precepts, whenever the life of the saints is either praised or blamed. But among the Christians there was only [error], or they are slandered as much as the demons whom they think are gods wish; as if it were difficult for anyone to recall what shameful and disgraceful things were performed in theaters and temples in service to the gods, and to attend to what is read, said, and heard in the churches, or what is offered to the true God; and from this to understand where the building and where the ruin of morals lies. But who said this to him or inspired it, except a diabolical spirit, such a vain and fit lie: that the demons prohibited from being worshipped by the Hebrews are revered rather than hated by Christians? But that God whom the wise men of the Hebrews worshipped—and the celestial holy angels and powers of God, whom we venerate and love as most blessed citizens in this our mortal pilgrimage—forbids sacrifice to be made [to others], thundering in his law which he gave to his Hebrew people; and he brought it in very threateningly, saying: He who sacrifices to gods shall be rooted out. And lest anyone should think it was commanded that sacrifice not be made to the most wicked demons and earthly spirits, whom that man <note>Porphyry</note> calls the least or lesser ones—since in the holy scriptures they themselves are called gods, not of the Hebrews

but of the Gentiles: which the seventy interpreters <note>The Septuagint: the Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> evidently placed in the psalm, saying: For all the gods of the Gentiles are demons. Lest anyone therefore should think it was prohibited to these demons indeed, but permitted to sacrifice to all or some of the celestial beings, he immediately added: except to the Lord alone; that is, except to the Lord only. Lest perhaps he who says "to the Lord alone" should believe that there is some other god to whom he thinks sacrifice should be made. That this is not to be so understood is very easily found in the Greek scriptures. Therefore the God of the Hebrews, to whom even this great philosopher <note>Porphyry</note> provides such great testimony, gave the law to his Hebrew people, written in the Hebrew language; not obscure and unknown, but now spread abroad among all nations, in which law it is written: He who sacrifices to gods shall be rooted out, except to the Lord only. What need is there to search for many things in this his law and his prophets concerning this matter? Rather, there is no need to search; for they are not hidden or rare things, but plain and frequent to collect and to place in this my disputation, by which it appears clearer than light that he willed sacrifice to be made to no one at all except to himself, the true and supreme God. Behold this one thing, briefly yet grandly, threateningly but truthfully said by that God whom the most learned of them preach as so excellent: let it be heard, let it be feared, let it be fulfilled, lest the rooting out of the disobedient follow. He who sacrifices to gods shall be rooted out, he says, except to the Lord only. Not because he has need of anything, but because it is expedient for us that we be his possession. For to him it is sung in the holy writings of the Hebrews: I have said to the Lord, you are my God, since you have no need of my goods. Moreover, we ourselves are his most noble and best sacrifice. This is his city, the mystery of which thing we celebrate with our offerings, which are known to the faithful, just as we have disputed in the preceding books. ### The Parable of the Wheat

A parable of a man who lived among the fields and did not know the ways of the city dwellers. He sowed wheat and ate the wheat in its raw form. One day he entered the city, and they brought him a good loaf of bread. He said, "What is this man-made thing for?" They said, "It is bread to eat." He ate it and found it very pleasant to his taste. **The Rabbi said**: This is made from the exalted. They said, "It is wheat." Later they brought him cakes kneaded in oil. He tasted them and said, "And these, what are they made of?" They said, "Wheat." Later they brought him royal pastries made with honey and oil. He said, "And these sweets, what are they made of?" They said, "Wheat." He said, "Surely I am the master of all these things, for I eat the essence of all these, which is wheat." And because of that...

Now we return to the distinction between their various sects and the explanation of each. Help, protection, and success are from God.

# Chapter on their various sects and schools, their signs, stations, and stories

I have mentioned previously in the account of Abu al-Hasan al-Nuri <note>may God have mercy on him</note> that they consist of twelve groups. <margin>D fol. 126a; B p. 58</margin> Two of them are rejected and ten are accepted. Each class among them possesses a beautiful way of dealing with God and a praised path in self-mortification <term>mujahadat</term> <gloss>spiritual struggles</gloss>, as well as a subtle etiquette in contemplation <term>mushahadat</term> <gloss>vision of the Divine</gloss>. Although they differ in their dealings, mortifications, contemplations, and ascetic practices, they are in agreement and accord regarding the principles and branches of the Religious Law and Divine Unity <term>tawhid</term>. <margin>B fol. 102v</margin> Abu Yazid <note>al-Bistami</note> <note>may God be pleased with him</note> said: The disagreement of the scholars is a mercy, except regarding the isolation of Divine Unity. A well-known tradition <note>hadith</note> agrees with this.

The reality of Sufism <term>tasawwuf</term> lies among the reports of the masters in terms of Truth <term>haqiqat</term>, and is divided in terms of metaphor and outward customs. Therefore, I shall speak briefly and concisely <margin>G fol. 124a</margin> to explain those divisions and spread out a carpet regarding the fundamental school of each one, so that the seeker may gain knowledge of it, the scholars may have a weapon, the disciples may find righteousness, and the lovers may find success.

<meta>continues from previous page: Like</meta> a section in which the Name **YHWH Elohim** <note>original: "יה'וה אלהים"; the combination of the Tetragrammaton and the Name associated with Judgment</note> is mentioned, these actions are performed through all the attributes that are completed by the Attribute of Judgment <note>Hebrew: *Middat ha-Din*</note> and the Attribute of Mercy <note>Hebrew: *Middat ha-Rakhamim*</note>. You will find this in the creation of the first man <note>Adam</note>, in his judgment, and in his expulsion; all these matters were conducted through both the Attribute of Judgment and the Attribute of Mercy. Everything was done in complete perfection, with mercy and judgment balanced as is fitting in a judgment of truth.

Based on this principle, the Torah states: "The Rock, His work is perfect" <note>Deuteronomy 32:4; original: "הצור תמים פעלו"</note>. The explanation of the verse is as follows: "The Rock" <note>Hebrew: *Ha-Tzur*</note> who decrees judgment with strength does not act with cruelty. He does not decree judgment until His work is "perfect" <note>Hebrew: *Tamim*</note>, meaning the judgment He decreed was first deliberated upon by the two attributes, Loving-kindness <note>Hebrew: *Chesed*</note> and Judgment <note>Hebrew: *Din*</note>. This is the meaning of "His work is perfect."

The term "perfect" <note>Hebrew: *Tamim*</note> is the secret of two things. It is as if it said "twins" <note>Hebrew: *Te'omim*</note>, but the language of honor uses the term *Tamim* for two things on high, while below it uses the term *Te'omim*. Thus it says: "And they shall be coupled <note>Hebrew: *Te'omim*</note> together below, and they shall be complete <note>Hebrew: *Tamim*</note> together on its top" <note>Exodus 26:24</note>. Below they are "twins," above they are "perfect." This is because below they appear as two distinct things, opposites like an advocate and an accuser. But above, everything is a single intention. Whether advocate or accuser, both have one purpose; there is no hatred or love there, and no favoritism, only a judgment of truth. Therefore it says "His work is perfect," for He consulted both Judgment and Mercy before decreeing the sentence. This is the secret of "True Judgment."

Regarding the phrase "For all His ways are justice" <note>Deuteronomy 32:4</note>, the explanation is that everything is visible to every eye, as it says "For all His ways are justice." You already know that Justice <note>Hebrew: *Mishpat*</note> is comprised of both Judgment and Mercy. Justice corresponds to Jacob, who is the Middle Pillar <note>Hebrew: *Ha-Kav ha-Emtza'i*</note> that mediates between the two "tents" of Abraham and Isaac. Abraham corresponds to Loving-kindness <note>Chesed</note>, Isaac corresponds to Judgment <note>Din</note>, and Jacob balances between them, as "a perfect man, dwelling in tents" <note>Genesis 25:27</note>. Justice corresponds to Jacob, drawing from Loving-kindness on Abraham's side and from Judgment on Isaac's side. Thus it says: "You have executed justice and righteousness in Jacob" <note>Psalm 99:4</note>.

The prophet said: "O Lord, correct me, but with justice; not in Your anger, lest You bring me to nothing" <note>Jeremiah 10:24</note>. The explanation of the verse "Correct me, O Lord, but with justice" <note>Hebrew: *Akh be-Mishpat*</note> is that the word "but" <note>Hebrew: *Akh*</note> acts as a divider, meaning: with the half of the attribute of Justice that is Loving-kindness. For Justice is half Judgment and half Loving-kindness. Therefore he said "but with justice," and followed with "not in Your anger, lest You bring me to nothing," revealing the secret of diminishing the half of Justice that stems from Anger.

Therefore, Justice is dependent on Jacob, who is the "father" among the tribes. He knew the great pain of children; when the Holy One, blessed be He, decrees against them, he seeks mercy and righteousness for them. The secret of "And the Lord of Hosts is exalted through justice" <note>Isaiah 5:16</note> is followed by "and the holy God is sanctified through righteousness." This means when Justice is exalted, Judgment is eased and turns toward the attribute of *El* <note>the Name associated with Chesed</note>. When "the Lord of Hosts is exalted through justice," the attribute of *El* which is above arrives and performs "righteousness" <note>Hebrew: *Tzedakah*</note>, and Justice is sweetened. This is the secret of the saying that Justice is included within Loving-kindness and Judgment, as it says: "You have executed justice and righteousness in Jacob."

The great secret is: "Righteousness and justice are the foundation of Your throne" <note>Psalm 89:15</note>. ### **Torah** Or <gloss>Torah Light</gloss> 
These commandments mentioned in this portion are divided into three parts, which are the three pillars upon which the world stands: Torah, Divine Service <term>Avodah</term>, and Acts of Loving-kindness <term>Gemilut Chasadim</term>. 

**Torah** consists of the prohibitions "Do not add" and "Do not subtract," which indicate the perfection of the Torah. This is as the philosophers have said: a thing that is absolutely perfect cannot be said to be lacking or redundant. For if it were lacking, it would not be perfect; and if it could accept an addition, it follows that it was not previously complete. Therefore, the definition of "perfect" is that which has neither deficiency nor excess. It is known that the Torah is dependent on His Great Name, which is <term>Y-H-V-H</term>, as in "The Torah of the Lord <note>Y-H-V-H</note> is perfect" <note>Psalm 19:8</note>, as I have elaborated in my commentary on Tractate Shevuot in the chapter "Torah Or." And as it says in the Zohar on the verse "This is My Name and this is My Memorial" <note>Exodus 3:15</note>: the letters <term>Y-H</term> with "My Name" <term>Shemi</term> equals 365 <note>The number of negative commandments</note>; the letters <term>V-H</term> with "My Memorial" <term>Zichri</term> equals 248 <note>The number of positive commandments</note>. It is written, "I am the first and I am the last" <note>Isaiah 44:6</note>; He is the absolute perfection, without subtraction or addition. Regarding this comes the warning: "You shall not do so to the Lord your God" <note>Deuteronomy 12:4</note>, which is a warning against erasing the Name or breaking a stone from the Holy Temple. Behold, the letters of the Name are in the House where He, may He be blessed, dwells; so too is the Sanctuary. It is written, "I am the Lord, that is My Name" <note>Isaiah 42:8</note>; the letters are like a frame for the House, and His Name, may He be blessed, is the soul within them. One who destroys His House, as it were, destroys Him. This is the secret of "You shall not do so to the Lord your God."

**Divine Service** <term>Avodah</term> comprises most of the commandments mentioned in this portion. The command came to have a fixed place in the Chosen House, and the text gives the reason: "To His habitation shall you seek, and there you shall come" <note>Deuteronomy 12:5</note>. "To His habitation" <term>Leshichno</term> alludes to the Divine Presence <term>Shekhinah</term>, which is the Palace of the Name <term>Y-H-V-H</term>. As it is said, "Do not fear, for she shall dwell within me," for in the Temple, the Glory <term>Kavod</term> is unified with the Beauty <term>Tiferet</term> of His people. This is "to place His Name there," which the Targum <note>Aramaic translation</note> renders as "to cause His Presence to dwell." And "round about the holy place the wicked walk" <note>Psalm 12:9</note>, referring to the shells of impurity <term>Kelipot</term>. Therefore: "Take heed to yourself lest you offer your burnt offerings in every place that you see" <note>Deuteronomy 12:13</note>.

### **Sometimes** 
sparks of holiness spread outward, and it is a commandment to return them and bring them inside. This is the secret of the commandment to bring the firstborn offerings from outside the city to the Chosen House. Then the branch returns to its root, and it is written of them: "There you shall offer" <note>Deuteronomy 12:14</note>, meaning there they shall have an ascent <term>aliyah</term> and not outside. Since the holiness resides in the Chosen House, which is in the Holy Land, we are commanded to "turn away from evil" by destroying all the places where the nations worshipped. One must uproot and eradicate them, and this was commanded specifically in the Holy Land. The secret of this alludes to the ten nations whose power is not that of idolaters <note>in the same way</note>. The matter is that nations in the Land of Israel, who are under the dominion of the Honorable Name, worship God by "cutting the shoots" <note>a metaphor for heresy</note>, and this is actual idolatry. However, those outside the Land are under the dominion of external forces. Just as there is a great prohibition against breaking a single stone of holiness, so conversely it is a great commandment to destroy and eliminate a "Subverted City" <term>Ir HaNidachat</term> and never to rebuild it, for its place is impure. Likewise, one who entices <term>Mesit</term> or misleads others must be uprooted, for he stems from the impurity of the ancient Serpent who was an enticer. The Holy One, blessed be He, immediately said, "Cursed is the Serpent"; therefore, the powers of the Left Side <term>Samael</term> are never appeased. The command came not to love him and not to listen to him, as was said regarding the Serpent: "I will put enmity between you and the woman" <note>Genesis 3:15</note>. A false prophet is also like an enticer. 

Let us return to the matter: the root of holiness is the Chosen House and Jerusalem. This is the reason for the first fruits <term>Bikkurim</term>, which the priests have no permission to eat until they are placed in the Chosen House. For the first fruits, being the "beginning," indicate great holiness, as I have written elsewhere. Therefore, they must go to the holy place, and from there they take their wisdom, for they are holy to God, and they shall eat in Jerusalem. The secret of "lesser holy" offerings and the Second Tithe <term>Ma'aser Sheni</term> is that they are eaten in Jerusalem. This is "your grain, your wine, and your oil," which are the primary ancestors of all sustenance. It is forbidden to eat lesser holy offerings until after the sprinkling of their blood, for the blood is the soul; afterward, permission is given to enjoy them. Know that just as the service of the sacrifice is an offering to God, so too is the worshiper, for the essence of the service is that one sacrifices himself, in the secret of "When a man <term>Adam</term> brings an offering from among you" <note>Leviticus 1:2</note>. The burnt offering <term>Olah</term> is entirely consumed, for it comes to atone for the thoughts of the heart, which are spiritual; it is offered all night so that the Serpent does not hinder it. Lesser holy offerings represent the peace of the soul and the body.

### **The secret** 
of the firstborn is the secret of the "Holy Israel," who are called "the firstborn of Israel." He has compassion on them and guards them, and they are called "the sheep of My pasture." Therefore, the firstborn is eaten only by the priests. The secret of eating consecrated items corresponds to those with blemishes... for Israel is holy and Israel is called "Man" <term>Adam</term>. He was originally holy, but afterward a blemish fell upon him after he sinned and was clothed in "garments of skin," but he has a redemption through the secret of "I will give a man in your stead." This was the secret of the Scapegoat <term>Azazel</term> which "bore their iniquities," meaning the iniquities that rest upon his head and his people. But we are commanded not to cause a blemish in a consecrated animal in order to eat it. For if one intentionally causes a blemish in holy things, he also violates the prohibition of working or shearing consecrated animals, for even the "broken tablets" <note>of the Ten Commandments</note> remain holy.

### **The general principle** 
is that the Service is the sacrifice, but the internal sacrifice is the Man himself. Likewise, his soul is called to the "Altar Above" after his death, and Michael is the High Priest. This is the secret, for "in the image of God was Man made." Therefore, the warning came to be careful during his life regarding damages to souls, not to kill a person except after thorough inquiry and investigation. Then he is "dead by the hand of Heaven," in the secret of "He is the witness, He is the judge," for the Lord, may He be blessed, is a True Witness and a True Judge. So must the Sanhedrin be: just as they are judges of truth, they must have witnesses of truth. I mean that they must clarify the truth of the witnesses with absolute clarity through inquiry and investigation; then their judgment is like the judgment of Heaven, and "precious in the eyes of the Lord is the death" <note>of His pious ones</note>.

### **And since** 
the death is precious in the eyes of the Lord—because Israel is holy from the side of their souls, which after death cleave to the realms above—therefore the command came: "You shall not cut yourselves, nor make any baldness..." <note>Deuteronomy 14:1</note>, for "you are children to the Lord your God." This is not the case for the nations; cutting and baldness are their customs, as is fitting for them, since at their death they go to destruction and have no portion in this world or the World to Come. We, however, are children of God. When we depart from this world, which is a temporary dwelling, we instead have a permanent residence above with our Father in Heaven. Therefore, it is forbidden to mourn excessively or perform these acts.

### **Let us return** 
to the matter: the person who worships is himself the sacrifice, as it says, "When a man brings an offering from among you." There is a further secret in this: for even when a person descends below through the secret of reincarnation <term>gilgul</term>—"Man and beast You save, O Lord" <note>Psalm 36:7</note>—therefore even in the eating of non-consecrated meat <term>basar ta'avah</term>, we were commanded regarding ritual slaughter <term>shechitah</term> with great care, without any nick in the blade. For if there is a nick, it becomes a carcass <term>nevelah</term>, and "a disgrace <term>nevalah</term> is committed in Israel." For who knows what reincarnation is within it? "Love your neighbor as yourself" <note>Leviticus 19:18</note>—choose for him a "beautiful death," namely, slaughter without a nick. If the animal dies on its own, the power of impurity takes hold of it. But when one slaughters it properly, and there is in the animal or the pure bird a spark of holiness, then its soul departs in purity.

### **One who eats** 
a limb from a living animal <term>ever min hachai</term> is like one who eats the flesh of a brother when a reincarnated soul is present. This is the secret of "You shall not eat the life with the flesh" <note>Deuteronomy 12:23</note>. Likewise, the prohibition of forbidden foods and the signs of pure animals, beasts, and birds all indicate the spark spread within them—whether it is from the Side of Impurity <term>Sitra Achra</term> or the Side of Holiness. I elaborated on this in Parashat Shemini. When Israel conducts themselves with holiness, it is written of them: "And they shall make for Me a sanctuary, and I will dwell among them" <note>Exodus 25:8</note>. For they themselves are the Tabernacle, as Man is divided into three parts: the head corresponds to the Holy of Holies; the heart corresponds to the Holy Place; and from the belly downward corresponds to the Courtyard, as I elaborated in Parashat Terumah. When one eats foods from the side of holiness, they are like an offering sacrificed upon the Altar. Regarding this, our Sages said: "Now, a man's table atones for him," as I have elaborated in its place.

### **Regarding** 
the commandments of the Festivals and their sacrifices, I have written about each in its specific place. The command came to rejoice on the festivals and to go up on the pilgrimage: "Three times a year shall all your males appear." Our Sages said: "Just as he comes to see, so he comes to be seen." Therefore, if one wishes to be seen in the Holy Temple where the Glory dwells, he must "turn from evil and do good" and be a faithful servant to his Creator. Otherwise, it is forbidden for a wicked person to enter the hall; how could he wish to be seen before Him, may He be blessed, and bring a burnt offering of appearance? For then he himself is a sacrifice through the sacrifice he offers. It says "Three times a year he shall appear"—Isaac, who was a "perfect burnt offering"...

### On the shame sought from unworthy praises.
## DIALOGUE XXVI.

> Praise sparingly, for when you praise unjustly,
> If you later condemn, it will be a sign of fickleness.

*Sorrow.* I am accused of having praised an unworthy man.
<note>A large ornamental initial L marks the beginning of Reason's response.</note>
*Reason.* I am accused of having praised an unworthy man. Indeed, an evil thing often arises from a good root. For the good and innocent, being such as they are, believe others to be the same. Hence they are even more prone to praise than is fair; and although I may admit it is bad to praise the unworthy, yet to disparage the undeserving is much worse.

*Sorrow.* I praised an unworthy man.

*Reason.* If you did so knowingly, you are blameworthy; but if unknowingly, you are excusable. It is a lesser evil to be deceived than to deceive. For to be deceived is the fault of another; but to deceive is the specific crime of the deceiver.

*Sorrow.* The praise of another turns into my infamy.

*Reason.* Rather, it is either your fault or your ignorance. For from another person, just as there is no true praise, so there is no true infamy.

*Sorrow.* I grieve greatly for having praised an unworthy man.

*Reason.* See to it then that you do not grieve for that very thing often. Beware lest you leap forward rashly to praise or to disparage. For there is a lust for both things: and (to speak properly) a certain disease and itch of a restless tongue that knows no quiet. First, if that happens, it does not happen in that part where the star itself consists of thick and solid fire, but where a thin splendor runs out and disperses into hair <note>original: "crines", referring to the comet's tail</note>. You see through the gaps between the fires, not through the fires themselves. He says, "All stars are round, but comets are elongated, from which it appears they are not stars." Who, indeed, will grant you that comets are long, when their nature is a globe just like the others? However, their brightness is extended just as the sun sends its rays far and wide. Yet the sun itself has one form, and the light flowing from it has another. Thus the body of comets itself is rounded, but their splendor appears longer than that of other stars.

"Why?" you ask. Tell me first why the moon receives a light so unlike the sun, though it receives it from the sun? Why is it sometimes red, sometimes pale? Why does it have a livid and black color when it is excluded from the sight of the sun? Tell me why all stars have a face somewhat unlike each other, and most different from the sun. Just as nothing prevents them from being stars even if they are not similar, so nothing prevents comets from being eternal and of the same condition as the rest, even if they do not have a similar face. Furthermore, if you consider the world itself, is it not composed of diverse things? Why is it that the sun always burns in Leo and scorches the lands with heat, but in Aquarius it binds the winter and closes the rivers with frost? Yet both this star and that are of the same condition <margin>† it rises</margin>, though they are dissimilar in effect and nature. In a very short time Aries <note>the Ram</note> is perfected <note>original: "excolitur", likely meaning it rises quickly</note>, while Libra sinks most slowly; and yet both this constellation and that are of the same nature, though one ascends in a brief time and the other is brought forth for a long duration.

Do you not see how contrary the elements are to each other? There are heavy and light things, cold and hot, moist and dry. The entire harmony of this world consists of discord. You deny that a comet is a star because its form does not correspond to the model, nor is it similar to the others. For you see, that star which returns to its place in the thirtieth year <note>Saturn</note> is very similar to this one which revisits its seat within a year. Nature does not perform its work according to a single form, but boasts in its very variety. It made some things slower, others faster than the rest. Some it made stronger, others more temperate; some it led out from the crowd so they might proceed as single and conspicuous things, while others it sent into a flock. He is ignorant of nature's power who thinks she is never permitted to do anything except what she does most often. She does not show comets frequently; she assigned them another place, other times, and motions unlike the rest. She wished to honor the magnitude of her work through these things, whose appearance is too beautiful for you to think them accidental, whether you consider their size or their brightness, which is greater and more burning than the others. Indeed, their appearance has something distinguished and singular, not cast into a narrow space and cramped, but let down more freely and embracing the region of many stars.

Aristotle says that comets signify storms and the intemperance of winds and rains. What then? Do you not judge that to be a star which announces future events? For there were very great and continuous storms everywhere; and in Achaia and Macedonia, cities were overthrown by earthquakes.

## Chapter Four: On the Common Rules for Vomiting and Purging, and an Indication of How to Attract the Purgative and Emetic Medicine

The person undergoing <term>evacuation</term> <gloss>istifrāgh; the removal of excess humors</gloss> must not rush to consume heavy or excessive foods, for <term>nature</term> <gloss>the body's innate healing power</gloss> will attract them while they are undigested. If any food is necessary, it must be taken little by little, spaced out so that it is gradual, ensuring that what enters the body is well-digested. <term>Phlebotomy</term> <gloss>bloodletting</gloss> is the evacuation specific to the blood itself. As for the evacuation specific to a <term>humor</term> <gloss>khilt</gloss> that is excessive in quantity or corrupted in quality, it is not achieved through bloodletting. Every excessive evacuation usually causes vomiting. If the cessation of a habitual bowel movement causes an illness, the remedy is usually to restore that evacuation; for example, if the cessation of a nosebleed or nasal discharge causes a blockage, its return will remove it. 

Know that the remaining matter that needs evacuation is less receptive to complete extraction; pursuing it until the patient's strength fails is dangerous. Often, <term>nature</term> dissolves that remainder on its own. As long as the humor is of the type that should be expelled and the patient can bear it, do not fear excess; sometimes you may even need to evacuate until <term>syncope</term> <gloss>fainting</gloss> occurs. If the patient's strength is robust but the bad humors are plentiful, evacuate them little by little. Likewise, if the matter is highly <term>mature</term> <gloss>nadj; ready for expulsion</gloss> or heavily mixed with the blood, it cannot be evacuated all at once, as is the case in <term>sciatica</term> <gloss>‘irq al-nasā</gloss>, chronic joint pains, cancer, chronic scabies, and chronic boils. 

Know that purging draws from above and uproots from below, which is consistent with the accustomed direction of attraction and suitable after the humors have settled. If the matter is below, drawing it in the opposite direction or uprooting it from its place is done through attraction and vice versa. The state of bloodletting varies according to the sites from which the blood is taken, as you have learned. Those who least need evacuation are those with good digestion, and inhabitants of hot countries have little need for evacuation.

We say: it is recommended for one who intends to take a purgative to restrict or divide their food intake for a period, and the first amount they try should be over several days, using various foods and various drinks. This state causes the stomach to desire to push what is in it either upward or downward. As for uniform food, the stomach becomes saturated and sluggish with it, gripping it tightly, especially if the amount is small. For those with naturally loose bowels, none of this is necessary. 

Know that the need for vomiting, purging, and the like does not occur in those who follow a <term>good regimen</term> <gloss>husn al-tadbīr</gloss>; they require lighter measures. Often, exercise, massage, and cupping are sufficient for them. If the body becomes full of the best of humors—meaning blood—then bloodletting is what is needed for cleansing, rather than purging. If necessity dictates bloodletting or evacuation in the autumn, one should begin with vomiting and delay bloodletting; this is among the counsels of Hippocrates and the writings of <term>Abila</term> <note>likely a reference to a commentator or specific medical authority</note>, and it is the truth. Likewise, if phlegmatic humors are mixed with the blood. However, if the humors are equal but viscous and cold, bloodletting may increase their thickness and viscosity; in such cases, one must begin with purging. 

In general, if the humors are equal, perform bloodletting first, then evacuate if any excess remains. If they are unequal, evacuate the excess first until they are equal, then perform bloodletting. Whoever prioritizes medicine over bloodletting should have performed bloodletting a few days prior. If someone has recently undergone bloodletting and needs evacuation, taking medicine will be more effective for them. Often, taking medicine when bloodletting was required results in vomiting and distress; if it does not settle with sedatives, then bloodletting should have preceded it. 

There is no evacuation required for excessive fullness that the severity of the illness and the fullness in quality and quantity do not call for. Often, a good regimen replaces the need for bloodletting at the time. Often, a cause calls for evacuation, but an obstacle arises, leaving no trick but sleep, fasting, and correcting the <term>dyscrasia</term> <gloss>sū’ mizāj; imbalance of temperament</gloss> caused by the fullness. Some evacuations are for the sake of precaution, such as what is needed by those prone to gout or epilepsy at a known time, especially in spring; they need to take precautions before the time and undergo the specific evacuation, whether bloodletting or purging. 

Sometimes the use of external drying agents and absorbent medicines acts as an evacuation, as is done for those with dropsy. You may need to use a medicine that matches the humor to be evacuated in quality, such as <term>scammony</term> <gloss>saqmūniyā</gloss> when you need to evacuate yellow bile; in that case, you must mix it with something that opposes it in quality but assists it in purging, such as <term>myrobalan</term> <gloss>halīlaj</gloss>. If a dyscrasia occurs afterward in those with internal tumors, their purging becomes weak; if forced, use things like <term>bindweed</term> <gloss>lablāb</gloss> and <term>safflower</term> <gloss>qartam</gloss>. 

As for the purgative and <term>cassia fistula</term> <gloss>khiyār shanbar</gloss>, Hippocrates said: "He whose constitution is easy to move should be treated with vomiting in the summer or spring, for that protects the body from exhaustion." Know that for one accustomed to loose bowels or unaccustomed to vomiting, taking a strong medicine is difficult and exhausting. An emetic medicine may turn into a purgative if the stomach is strong, or if taken during intense hunger, or if the person has loose bowels, or if the medicine is of a heavy substance that descends quickly. Conversely, a purgative may become an emetic due to a weak stomach, extreme heaviness, the medicine being repulsive, or the person having indigestion. 

Every purgative medicine, if it does not purge due to lack of <term>maturation</term> <gloss>nadj</gloss>, will stir the humor it is meant to purge and spread it through the body, overwhelming the system and drawing other humors to it, thus increasing that humor in the body. Some humors are quicker to respond to vomiting, such as yellow bile; others are resistant to vomiting, such as black bile. Some, like phlegm, are better suited for purging. For those whose humor is descending, such as those with <term>lientery</term> <gloss>zalaq al-am‘ā’; slippery intestines</gloss>, the intestines contract and hinder the purgative medicine. If the medicine is composed of widely differing ingredients in their purging time, the purging becomes disordered; the first may purge the second before the second can act, or the first may purge the second itself. 

Whoever undergoes purging while their body is clean will inevitably suffer from medicine-induced colic and distress, and the evacuation will be very difficult. In general, when medicine evacuates waste, there is no distress; if it is taken with distress, it is either evacuating something other than waste, or the humor being evacuated has changed, indicating the body is cleared of the intended humor.

### Question 85, Article 3: Whether more universal things are prior in our intellectual knowledge.

Third article: whether more universal things are prior in our intellectual knowledge.

Regarding the third, the procedure is as follows. It seems that more universal things are not prior in our intellectual knowledge: because those things which are prior and better known according to nature are posterior and less known to us; but universals are prior according to the nature of our intellect. Furthermore, composite things are prior to us compared to simple things, but universals are simpler, therefore they are known later by us. Furthermore, the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> says in the first book of the Physics that the defined thing first falls into our knowledge, and the parts of the definition are less universal: just as "animal" is a part of the definition of "man," and universals are known later by us. Furthermore, we arrive at effects by chance and principles, but universals are known later by us. But on the contrary is what is said in the first book of the Physics, that we must proceed from universals to singulars.

I respond that it must be said that in the knowledge of our intellect two things must be considered. First, indeed, that intellectual knowledge in some way takes its beginning from sensitive knowledge; and because the sense is of singulars and the intellect is of universals, it is necessary that the knowledge of singulars is prior to us than the knowledge of universals. Second, it must be considered that our intellect proceeds from potency to act. And that which proceeds from potency to act first reaches an incomplete act, which is the middle between potency and act, and then a perfect act. The perfect act to which the intellect reaches is complete science, through which things are known distinctly and determinately; the incomplete act is imperfect science, through which things are known indistinctly under a certain confusion. For what is known in this way is known both in act and in a certain way in potency. As the Philosopher says in the first book of the Physics: things that are confused are first manifest and certain to us; later, however, we know by distinguishing the principles and elements distinctly. 

It is manifest, however, that to know something in which many things are contained, without having proper knowledge of each of those things contained in it, is to know something under a certain confusion. In this way, both a whole in which parts are contained in potency and an integral whole can be known; for either whole can be known in a certain confusion without the parts being distinctly known. To know distinctly that which is contained in the whole is to have knowledge of a less common thing: just as to know "animal" indistinctly is to know "animal" in which there is either "rational" or "irrational," which is to know "man" or "lion." Therefore, it first occurs to our intellect to know "animal" before knowing "man." And the same reasoning holds if we compare any more universal thing to a less universal one. As the sense goes out from potency into act, so does the intellect: and this order

<column-break/>

of knowledge appears in the sense. For we judge more by sense when a thing is less known at a distance, perceiving it to be a body; and then perceiving it to be an animal; and then perceiving it to be a man; and finally perceiving it to be Socrates. Or it is clear that a child from the beginning first distinguishes "man" from "not-man"; and children from the beginning call all men "fathers." Later, however, they determine each one specifically, as is said in the first book of the Physics. Things are manifest, and he who knows something indistinctly is still in potency to knowing the specific difference and the principle, just as he who knows the genus is in potency to knowing the differences. And thus, indistinct knowledge is the medium between potency and act. And that the knowledge of singulars is prior to us in sensitive knowledge, and the knowledge of universals is prior in intellectual knowledge. If we compare sense with intellect, the more universal knowledge is prior to the knowledge of the less universal and common.

To the first, it must be said that it can be considered in two ways. In one way, as the intention of truth is considered. And since the intention of truth is true and the same, it has a relationship to many things. It comes through the abstraction of the intellect as an end in this way, while truly being posterior. In the first book *On the Soul* <note>Aristotle, De Anima</note>, it is said that the universal is either nothing or it is posterior; but Plato placed universals as substances; and in this consideration it is true, because particulars are nothing except by participation in the more universal subsisting things which are called Ideas. In another way, it can be considered regarding the nature itself of "animality" or "humanity" as it is found in particulars. And thus there is a twofold order of nature. One according to the way of generation and time, since in that way those things which are imperfect and in potency are prior. And in this way the more universal is prior in nature, which appears manifestly in the generation of man and animal. For first "animal" is generated before "man," as is said in the book *On the Generation of Animals*. The other is the order of perfection or the intention of nature, just as act is simply prior in nature, and that which is perfect is prior to that which is imperfect; and in this way the less universal is prior in nature, as "man" is prior to "animal." For the intention of nature does not stop at the generation of an animal, but intends to generate a man.

To the second, the more universal is compared to the less universal as a whole, and through the whole which is made, the more universal contains not only "man" and "horse" but others; just as "animal" contains not only "man" but also "rational." Thus, therefore, "animal" considered in itself is prior in our knowledge to "man." If "man" is prior in our knowledge to "animal," it is through his specific reasoning.

To the third, it must be said that something can be known in two ways. In one way absolutely, according to what it is in itself, and thus nothing is known. In another way, as they are parts of this whole, like stones; it is necessary that we first know the whole before the parts. For we first know the house in a certain confused way. Thus, therefore, it must be said that the defining parts, considered absolutely, are prior to us than the defined thing. Otherwise, the defined thing would not be made known through them. But they are more like parts.

<summary>Thomas Aquinas discusses the order of human understanding, arguing that intellectual knowledge moves from the universal and confused to the particular and distinct. He reconciles this with the fact that sensory knowledge begins with singular objects, explaining that the intellect proceeds from potency to act.</summary>
<keywords>universals, singulars, intellect, potency and act, Aristotle, generation, definition, cognition</keywords>

# Kalila and Dimna

When the Lion woke the next morning, the Judge and a group of his prominent companions entered his presence with a written record of what Dimna had said in his <term>ma'adhir</term> <gloss>excuses or legal defenses</gloss>. The Lion took the document and ordered them to depart from him.

Then he sent for his mother and read the document to her. It distressed her, and she said: "If I am harsh with you, O King, do not be angry."

The Lion said: "I shall not be angry, so say what you wish."

She said: "I do not see you recognizing what harms you from what benefits you. I believe that as long as you continue to delay and deliberate over Dimna's case, he will stir up against you a trouble that you will be unable to withstand, whether sitting or standing."

Then she stood up and left in anger. When the next day came, the Judge sent for Dimna and brought him out. He consulted the <term>ulama</term> <gloss>scholars or learned men</gloss> regarding him, but they said nothing.

The Judge said to him: "Even if all those present are silent and say nothing, their suspicions have converged on the fact that you are a criminal. There is no good for you in life after this accusation has taken root in their hearts. I see nothing better for you than to confess your guilt. By doing so, you would save your soul from the consequences of the afterlife, and you would regain a good reputation for two reasons: first, your ability to find ways out and to devise <term>ma'adhir</term> <gloss>excuses</gloss> to defend yourself; and second, your voluntary confession of your sin, choosing safety in the afterlife over safety in this world. For the scholars have said: Death in a state of beauty is better than life in a state of ugliness."

Dimna answered him, saying: "Judges do not pass judgment based on their own suspicions, nor on the suspicions of the common people or the elite. I have learned that suspicion is no substitute for the truth. Even if you all suspect that I am the perpetrator of this crime, I know myself best, and my knowledge of myself is a certainty in which there is no doubt. My situation has only become ugly in your eyes because you have assumed that I acted with malice."

<summary>The Lion's mother warns him against Dimna's cunning while the Judge pressures Dimna to confess his crimes to save his soul. Dimna maintains his innocence, arguing that legal judgments must be based on certainty rather than public suspicion.</summary>

# The Turmoil in the Mind of the Sultan of Tirmidh

A clamor arose throughout the entire <term>divan</term> <gloss>royal court</gloss>;
The turmoil in the mind of that Sultan grew.
The hearts of both the elite and the commoners of the city were lost,
Wondering what distress and calamity had occurred.
"Is a powerful enemy intending to attack us,
Or has a celestial plague arisen from the Unseen?"
For <term>Dalqak</term> <gloss>the Jester</gloss> had arrived in a great rush,
Killing several <term>Tazi</term> <gloss>Arabian</gloss> horses along the way.
The people gathered at the King’s palace:
"Why has he come with such frantic haste?"
From his speed, a foul diligence was perceived;
A roar and agitation filled the city of Tirmidh.
One person raised both hands in prayer,
While another, out of anxiety, wailed "Alas!"
From the outcry, the sedition, the fear, and the punishment,
Every heart wandered through a hundred kinds of imaginings.
Everyone made a prediction based on their own conjecture:
"What fire has fallen into the felt garment <note>meaning: what disaster has struck the kingdom</note>?"
The King quickly sought a path and gave him entry;
When he kissed the ground, the King said: "Hey, what happened?"
To whoever asked him of his state, that sour-faced man
Put a finger to his lips, saying: "Hush!"
His cleverness only inflamed the King’s suspicion;
Everyone became stunned and silent in the agitation.
The Jester gestured: "O Munificent King,
Leave me for a moment so I may catch my breath,
Until my fleeting intellect returns to me,
For I have fallen into a wondrous world."
After an hour, during which the King’s throat and mouth
Turned bitter from the suspicion of his thoughts—
For he had never seen the Jester in such a state,
As there was no companion more pleasant than him;
He used to constantly display tricks and jests,
Keeping the King happy and laughing.
He would make the King laugh so much in his seat
That the King would clutch his belly, doubled over,
Until his body would break into a sweat from the force of laughter,
And he would fall on his face from the intensity of it.
Yet today, he is thus pale and sour-faced,
Pressing a finger to his lips: "O King, be silent!"
Suspicion upon suspicion, and fantasy upon fantasy:
"What punishment will befall the King?"
For the King’s heart was filled with grief and caution,
Because the <term>Khwarazm-Shah</term> <gloss>Ruler of Khwarazm</gloss> was very bloodthirsty.
He had killed many kings of that region,
Either by guile or by the power of that stubborn one.
This King of Tirmidh was already in a state of suspicion,
And by the Jester’s artifice, that suspicion increased.
He said: "Speak quickly! What is the situation?
From whom is this turmoil and agitation of yours?"
He replied: "I heard in the village that the King
Has sent a herald to every crossroads,
Saying: 'I want someone who, in three days,
Can reach Samarkand and return, even now.
I have set aside treasures for him in exchange,
When the purpose of the message is achieved.'
I hurried to him for that reason,
To say: 'I do not have that ability.'
Such a lowly task does not suit one like me;
Do not weave the thread of this hope upon me."

Last night, a sharp-witted man of experience told me in secret,
