Isa ibn Hisham narrated to us, saying:
I turned with a group of my companions to the courtyard of a tent seeking hospitality from its people. A man with a parched complexion came out to us and said: "Who are you?" We said: "Guests who have not tasted an enemy <note>meaning: food</note> for three days." He said: "Move aside." Then he said: "O youths, what do you think of a portion of <term>nahida</term> <gloss>a dish of butter and flour</gloss> as white as a bald man's pate, in a wide bowl, crowned with the choice froth from the sides of a great, sturdy camel, one portion of which fills the mouth, for a group of hungry, thirsty men who have traveled five days, in which the tooth disappears, whose date-stones are like the tongues of birds? They gulp down the <term>nahida</term> with bowls of milk they have milked from old, sturdy camels. Do you desire it, O youths?" We said: "Yes, by God, we desire it!" The old man guffawed and said: "And your uncle <note>referring to himself</note> also desires it!" 

Then he said: "What is your opinion, O youths, of fine white bread like pieces of silver ingots, arranged on a leather mat smelling of mimosa bark? He goes to the <term>ghada</term> wood and kindles the fire. When its flame dies down, he prepares its embers, then takes his dough and throws it in after perfecting its color. He spreads it over the embers, then covers it until it puffs up and glows. He heaps upon it hot stones until the two heats meet, until he covers them on the matching embers with a lid. You set the share as one hundred and nine parts, then multiply thirteen by one hundred and nine parts and add eighty parts to that. The total becomes one thousand four hundred and ninety-seven, and the husband's portion is three hundred and twenty-seven.

If a woman leaves two sisters and a husband, and bequeaths to a man the equivalent of a sister's portion minus one-eighth of what remains of the estate after the legacy, the calculation for this is to establish the <term>faridah</term> <gloss>legal distribution of inheritance</gloss> from twelve shares. Each sister receives one-third of what remains of the estate after the legacy. This is the estate minus the legacy. You know that one-eighth of what remains plus the legacy equals a sister's portion. One-eighth of what remains is one-eighth of the estate minus one-eighth of the legacy. Therefore, one-eighth of the estate minus one-eighth of the legacy plus the legacy equals a sister's portion. This is equivalent to one-eighth of the estate and seven-eighths of the legacy. The entire estate then equals three-eighths of the estate plus three legacies and five-eighths of a legacy. Subtract three-eighths of the estate from the whole estate, and five-eighths of the estate remains, equaling three legacies and five-eighths of a legacy. Thus, the whole estate equals five legacies and four-fifths of a legacy. The estate is twenty-nine, the legacy is five, and the portion is eight.

In another type of legacy: a man dies and leaves four sons, and bequeaths to a man the equivalent of the portion of one of his sons, and to another man one-quarter of what remains of the third. Know that the legacy is only taken from the third.

<meta>continues from previous page: As for the error that occurs from someone other than this class of people, it is pure sin.</meta>

Pure sin, whether the error is in theoretical or practical matters. Just as an ignorant judge who is unfamiliar with the <term>Sunnah</term> <gloss>the traditions and practices of the Prophet</gloss> is not excused if he errs in a ruling, so too the one who judges concerning existing things is not excused if he does not meet the conditions for judgment. Rather, he is either a sinner or an infidel. 

If it is required of a judge in matters of the permitted and the forbidden that the means of <term>ijtihad</term> <gloss>independent legal reasoning</gloss> be gathered in him—which is the knowledge of the <term>usul</term> <gloss>legal fundamentals</gloss> and the knowledge of <term>istinbat</term> <gloss>deduction</gloss> from those fundamentals by <term>qiyas</term> <gloss>analogy</gloss>—how much more so should this be required for the one who judges existing things? I mean that he must know the rational first principles and the method of deduction from them. 

In short, error regarding the Law is of two kinds. First, an error for which a person is excused if they are among those qualified to investigate the matter in which the error occurred, just as a skilled physician is excused if he errs in the art of medicine, or a skilled judge if he errs in a judgment; however, one who is not an expert in that field is not excused. 

Second, there is an error for which no one is excused. If it occurs regarding the principles of the Law, it is <term>kufr</term> <gloss>infidelity or unbelief</gloss>, and if it occurs in matters beyond the principles, it is <term>bid'ah</term> <gloss>innovation</gloss>. This type of error concerns things that all classes of argumentative methods lead to knowing, such that knowledge of that thing is possible for everyone. This includes the acknowledgment of God, Blessed and Exalted is He, the Prophethoods, and happiness or misery in the afterlife. This is because these three foundations are reached by the three types of evidence which <note>The three types of evidence refer to the rhetorical, dialectical, and demonstrative methods mentioned earlier in the text.</note>

<summary>Averroes argues that only qualified scholars are excused for errors in complex legal or philosophical interpretations. He defines fundamental tenets of faith—God, Prophecy, and the Afterlife—as being so clearly provable that error regarding them constitutes infidelity.</summary>

Even with his right paw pinned, he broke a thousand splinters and a thousand fragments of the spears aimed and hurled at him from above. Half-dead and bloodless, he filled those watching with dread, wondering what he might have done if he were free and unharmed. A certain Juan de Ledesma of Seville, a friend of Vasco <note>Vasco Núñez de Balboa</note> and a companion in his labors, confessed that he had eaten of that tiger. After the male tiger was killed, they followed his tracks toward the mountains and reached the cave that was his conjugal home.

In the absence of the mother, they carried off two cubs that were not yet old enough to be weaned from their mother's teats. The Arabs used to say: "Shine, Thabir <note>a mountain overlooking the valley</note>, so that we may depart," in opposition <note>to the Islamic practice of departing after sunset</note>. It is also called Jam'ah and al-Mash'ar al-Haram <gloss>The Sacred Monument</gloss>.

Arafah is a village containing farms, greenery, and melon fields. It has fine houses belonging to the people of Mecca where they stay on the Day of Arafah. The standing place <note>for the pilgrimage ritual</note> is at its morning side near Mount Mutalat. There are watering places there, a canal that flows through it, and a landmark built behind the Imam for the supplication, with the people gathered around him and on the nearby mountains. 

The prayer hall <note>al-Musalla</note> is on the edge of the Wadi Urana at the borders of Arafah. Standing in the valley itself is not permitted; whoever enters it before sunset must offer a blood sacrifice <note>as an expiation</note>. White landmarks mark the boundary of Arafah. In the prayer hall is a pulpit made of brick, and behind it is a large basin. Two miles before it are the Mazamayn <gloss>the two narrow passes</gloss>, which mark the boundary of the Sacred Territory <note>al-Haram</note>. Batn Muhassir is a valley between Mina and al-Muzdalifa, and it is the border of al-Muzdalifa.

Al-Tan'im is a place containing several mosques around the Mosque of Aisha, along with watering places on the road to Medina. From here, the residents of Mecca enter the state of <term>ihram</term> <gloss>ritual consecration</gloss> for the <term>Umrah</term> <gloss>lesser pilgrimage</gloss>. White landmarks surround the Sacred Territory. From the western road at al-Tan'im, the distance is three miles; from the Iraq road, nine miles; from the Yemen road, seven miles; from the Ta'if road, eleven miles; and from the main highway, ten miles.

Dhu al-Hulayfa is a village near Yathrib <gloss>Medina</gloss> containing a flourishing mosque. There are wells nearby, but no houses are seen there. Al-Juhfa is a city inhabited by the Banu Ja'far. It has a fortification with two gates and a few wells. Two miles away is a spring and a large pool, though water may sometimes be scarce there, and it is plentiful <unclear>at other times</unclear>.

This is a great affliction <term>afa</term> <gloss>a blight or harmful influence</gloss> for which reason everyone who plunges into those sciences must be restrained. For even if they do not relate to matters of religion, since they are among the foundations of their <note>the philosophers'</note> sciences, their evil and ill-fortune spread <gloss>Note 70: In version "Sh" it reads: "it spreads."</gloss> to the student. Few are those who plunge into them without stripping off the garment of religion and undoing the bridle of piety from their heads.

**The Second Affliction:** This arises from an ignorant friend of Islam who imagines that religion must be supported by denying every science attributed to them <note>the philosophers</note>. Thus, he denies all their sciences and claims they are ignorant in them, even denying their statements regarding solar and lunar eclipses, asserting that what they say is contrary to the Divine Law <term>Shari'a</term>. When this reaches the ear of someone who knows those matters by definitive proof <term>burhan qati'</term>, he does not doubt his proof, but rather believes that Islam is built upon ignorance and the denial of definitive proof. Consequently, his love for philosophy increases and his hatred for Islam grows. Great indeed is the crime against religion committed by those who imagine that Islam is supported by the denial of these sciences. The Divine Law does not address these sciences by way of either denial or affirmation, nor do these sciences address religious matters. The Prophet—peace and blessings be upon him—said:

> The sun and the moon are two of the signs of God the Exalted. They do not eclipse for the death or life of anyone. So when you see that,

This, then, is the judgment on mathematics and its affliction.

The Light of the world is for the natural or external man, and thus for those things which are in him. Although the things there do not appear to belong to that light, they nevertheless do; for nothing can be grasped by the natural man except through such things as exist and appear in the solar world, and thus unless they have some form from the light and shade there. All ideas of time and ideas of space, which are so important in the natural man that he cannot think without them, also belong to the light of the world. But the Light of heaven is for the spiritual or internal man. The interior mind of man, where his intellectual ideas—which are called immaterial—reside, is in that light. Man is unaware of this, even though he calls his intellect "sight" and ascribes "light" to it. The reason is that as long as he is in worldly and corporeal things, he only has a perception of such things as belong to the light of the world, but not of such things as belong to the light of heaven. Regarding the statement "I do not perceive any phenomenon that attains perfect awakening, nor any phenomenon through which one attains perfect awakening," this means that although I understand all phenomena in every aspect through conventional knowledge subsumed within the wisdom of omniscience, when analyzed through ultimate wisdom, no phenomenon that knows or is to be known is seen, just like objects seen in a dream.

The phrase "O sons of the gods, because all phenomena are utterly pure" means that in this context, "purity" refers to the very absence of any entity. It is a synonym for "utterly non-existent."

The statement "O Blessed One, it is not difficult to attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening" is made because all phenomena are non-existent. It is not difficult to realize that a non-entity is a non-entity. However, it would be difficult to realize the true nature of phenomena if they actually existed. It is not difficult to know and accomplish the non-existence of what is already non-existent. If phenomena existed, one would need to accomplish the practices of the <term>paramitas</term> <gloss>perfections</gloss> and so forth in order to increase virtuous qualities and abandon non-virtuous qualities. Since these phenomena do not exist, the accomplishment is not difficult. Therefore, it is said that "attaining perfect awakening is not difficult."

The intention behind the Elder Shariputra’s statement that attaining perfect awakening is difficult is as follows: If it were enough to simply remain in silence after realizing that all phenomena are of the nature of non-entities, being non-existent like space, then it would not be difficult. However, one must realize that in reality there is no perfect awakening of any phenomenon, and yet subsequently engage in the practices of the perfections and perfectly awaken to all phenomena.

# The Explanation of the Noble Four Dharmas

Homage to Mañjuśrī, the Ever-Youthful.

Why was this <term>sutra</term> <gloss>scriptural discourse</gloss> composed, which states: "A <term>bodhisattva mahasattva</term> <gloss>great heroic being seeking awakening</gloss> should not abandon these four <term>dharmas</term> <gloss>qualities or practices</gloss> for as long as they live, even for the sake of their life"?

It was composed to correctly show the method for attaining unsurpassed awakening to those who are confused about entering the <term>Mahayana</term> <gloss>Great Vehicle</gloss>. It is to cause those who are heedless to correctly adopt the practice. It is to correctly encourage those who are discouraged. It is to cause those who have correctly entered the path to be truly joyful.

The number "four" is mentioned to prevent the refusal of those who might be reluctant to listen due to a fear of excessive length. Mentioning the number allows for easy recollection. Furthermore, the qualities of patience and gentleness, which appear below, share a single purpose and are thus not differentiated.

Although there are many categories of those who have correctly entered the Great Vehicle, two names <note>Bodhisattva and Mahasattva</note> are mentioned for three reasons: due to their aspiration, their application, and their realization.

How is it due to aspiration? They are called a <term>bodhisattva</term> <gloss>awakening-being</gloss> because they aspire toward profound objects of knowledge. They are called a <term>mahasattva</term> <gloss>great being</gloss> because they aspire toward great power.

How is it due to application? It is because they exert themselves for the sake of their own unsurpassed, perfect awakening, and for the sake of completely protecting all sentient beings from suffering.

How is it due to realization? It is because awakening is realized through two strengths. Which two? The strength of intelligence and the strength of diligence. One cannot realize awakening through ignorance or through small diligence.

### ON ALCHEMY.

<margin>The end of Alchemy is not gold and silver, but secrets.</margin>

<margin>Poison even in the best things.</margin>
Who is there who would dare to deny that poison lies hidden and exists even in the best things? Everyone is compelled to confess this. If this is true, then I ask you now: must the poison not be separated from the good and the useful? And the good accepted, the evil left behind? Indeed, it must be so. If it must be so, I ask you, tell me: how is it separated in your workshops? For with you, everything remains mixed together. But so that you may protect your simplicity, if you are convicted into confessing that poison lies hidden there, and are asked where it finally goes: then you bring forth I know not what about "corrections" which are supposed to drive out and take away the poison, <margin>The correction of the Physicians is examined.</margin> just as they say Quinces correct Scammony, and afterwards <term>Diagridium</term> <gloss>a preparation of scammony juice</gloss>. But what kind of correction is that? Does the poison not remain afterward just as it was at first? And yet you meanwhile boast that you have corrected it, so much so that the poison no longer harms. But where did it escape to? <margin>Diagridion.</margin> It remains in the Diagridium. Try it, if you are wise: exceed the limit, and you will see where the poison is. For you will know it soon enough. Thus you also correct <term>Turbith</term> <gloss>a medicinal root</gloss>, and you call it <term>Diaturbith</term>. Such are your corrections, which would be fit for peasants and should be given to pack-horses. Make the danger by exceeding the limit and increase the dose: you will see whether you do not feel the poison. <margin>What it is to correct a Medicine.</margin> *To correct is to take what has been corrected.* He who is malicious and has sinned: if he is punished, the correction does not extend further than the will of him who was punished lasts. Such are these corrections also; the power lies with the substances themselves, not with you. Now indeed, in this case, a Physician must consider nothing further than that the poison be removed. This must be done through separation. As, for example: a serpent is poisonous, and yet it is adopted for food. If you remove the poison from it, you may eat it with no harm. The same must be understood equally concerning all other things, namely that there is need for a similar separation. Until that is done, you cannot be secure in your operation, unless by chance it happens that nature supplies your deficiencies, or a greater benevolence of the heavens favors you. For in your art, no protection will have remained.

Now therefore, at last, if that true foundation which removes poison is required, let us see how Alchemy provides it. For it is necessary that it be done in this way: if Mars <note>the metal iron or the planetary influence</note> is in the Sun <note>gold</note>, Mars must be removed; and if Saturn <note>lead</note> is found in Venus <note>copper</note>, it must be separated from her. For as many ascendants and impressions as there are in the things of nature, so many bodies also exist in them. But those bodies which are contrary, it is entirely necessary that some of them be removed and taken away, so that in this way all contrariety is abolished, and from the good, the evil which you seek to avoid is taken away. <margin>Fire perfects all things.</margin> Just as gold is useful for nothing unless it is first cast into the fire, so a Medicine is much less useful which does not pass through the fire. For it is necessary for all things to pass through the fire into a second generation, by which it ought to benefit and help man. And should this not deservedly be judged the honest foundation of any Physician? For a Physician ought not to apply poisons, but <term>arcana</term>. <margin>The workshops are rebuked.</margin> However, all those preparations of the workshops <note>the apothecary shops</note>, as many as there are, do not contribute even a single letter to this doctrine. Instead, they are occupied simply in "correcting," as if a dog farted in a room, and that stench were suppressed either by lozenges and incense, or by juniper wood: I ask you, does the stench not remain in the room afterward just as much as before? And although it may not be perceived by the sense of smell, is it therefore lawful for anyone to say the stench has been separated and no longer remains? Indeed it is present, but corrected by the fumigation. Thus the fumigation and the foul air enter the nostrils together. Of this kind also are the corrections of the Pharmacists, who blunt an <term>Aleopaticum</term> <gloss>a bitter or purging medicine</gloss> with sugar, so that it inflicts no harm. Thus sugar and honey are their <term>magistery</term> <gloss>master-work</gloss>. Thus they also "correct" gentian with treacle. Are these not truly the works of asinine ignorance? Yet they boast and sell themselves as the Physicians of princes. Who indeed is so stupid as not to smell immediately that these things are worthless? What else, I ask, can they boast about their remedies, except to say, *This Electuary is sweet, made of spices and sugar,*
